unit.title: Provide advice on retail beauty care products

theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: Why does a salon give clients advice on retail products?
options: So the client must buy something before leaving the salon
So the client can care for their hair or skin at home
So the stylist can sell the most costly item on the shelf
So the salon can clear old stock that is close to expiry

questions.stem: Good retail advice for a client should be based mainly on:
options: the product that gives the salon the biggest profit
the product the stylist likes to use on their own hair
the product with the most colourful advertising
the needs found in the client's consultation

questions.stem: Shanice had a relaxer at the salon today. Why should her stylist suggest products for home care?
options: To help keep her relaxed hair healthy until the next visit
To make sure she never needs to come back to the salon
To let her do her own relaxer touch-ups safely at home
To use up the free samples the supplier left at the front desk

questions.stem: On a product label, where is the ingredient used in the largest amount usually listed?
options: Last, at the end of the list
In the middle of the list
First, at the start of the list
On a separate leaflet inside the box

questions.stem: What is a 'feature' of a product?
options: The good result the client gets from using it
The price the client pays for it at the desk
A fact about what the product is or contains
The way the salon puts it on the display shelf

questions.stem: A conditioner contains shea butter. Which statement is a 'benefit' for the client?
options: It helps her dry hair feel softer and easier to comb
It comes in a 250 ml bottle with a pump on the top
It is made by a company that started many years ago
It is kept on the second shelf near the front desk

questions.stem: Which skin type usually looks shiny all over and has large, open pores?
options: Dry skin
Sensitive skin
Mature skin
Oily skin

questions.stem: A client says her skin feels tight after washing and has rough, flaky patches. Which product type suits her best?
options: A strong drying lotion for spots
A rich moisturiser for dry skin
A grainy scrub to use twice a day
An oil-free mattifying gel

questions.stem: What does the SPF number on a sunscreen tell the client?
options: How well it protects the skin from sunburn
How many months it can be kept on the shelf
How much colour it adds to the skin
How strong its scent is on the skin

questions.stem: Why should a client use a heat protection product before using a flat iron at home?
options: To make the flat iron heat up much more quickly
To let her use the iron on wet, dripping hair
To help reduce heat damage to the hair
To make the hair colour last longer

questions.stem: Which is an open question to use when finding out a client's needs?
options: Do you want to buy a new shampoo today?
How does your hair feel after washing?
Is your skin oily by the middle of the day?
Have you used this cream before?

questions.stem: Why should the therapist listen carefully and let the client finish speaking?
options: So the therapist has time to think of a sales joke
So the client feels rushed and buys more quickly
So the therapist can talk about her own products
To find the real needs and show the client respect

questions.stem: Where should the products a client buys, and any reactions she has, be recorded?
options: On a sticky note on the mirror
In the stylist's personal phone
On the back of the receipt only
On the client's record card

questions.stem: A client says she is allergic to nuts. What should you check before suggesting a hair oil?
options: The price shown on the shelf label
The ingredient list on the label
The size and shape of the bottle
How many bottles are left in stock

questions.stem: A client shows you red, weeping, broken skin on her face and asks for a strong scrub. What should you do?
options: Not sell the scrub and advise her to see a doctor
Sell the scrub and tell her to use it gently
Give her a free sample to try on the area tonight
Sell a stronger scrub so it clears up faster

questions.stem: A client wants to buy a hair dye to use at home. What should you advise her to do first?
options: Mix it with a different brand to make it gentler
Leave it on longer than the instructions say
Do a skin test as the maker's instructions say
Put it on straight away if her scalp feels itchy

questions.stem: Many hair-dye makers ask for a skin test to be done how long before the colour is used?
options: About 48 hours
About 5 minutes
About 2 weeks
About 1 hour

questions.stem: What is 'link selling' in a salon?
options: Selling products only through a website link
Selling a product the client says she does not need
Selling stock to another salon at a discount
Suggesting a product that goes with a service

questions.stem: After a manicure, which product is the best link sale?
options: A clarifying shampoo for oily hair
A foot file for hard skin
A cuticle oil and hand cream
A setting lotion for curls

questions.stem: How should a cream be taken from a display jar to show a client?
options: With a clean finger, dipped in once
With a clean spatula, used once
With the client's own fingers
By pouring it from the jar on the hand

questions.stem: Where is a good place to show a client a small amount of a hand cream?
options: On a scratch on her finger
On the back of her hand
On the skin under her eye
On a rash on her wrist

questions.stem: Why should you explain to the client how much product to use and how often?
options: So she runs out quickly and must buy more
So she can ignore the instructions on the label
So she gets the best result and uses it safely
So she can share it with all of her family

questions.stem: A client buys a strong leave-in treatment. The label says to use it once a week. She asks if she can use it every day. What should you say?
options: Yes, more often will work faster
Yes, but only on her ends and roots
Yes, if she uses less each time
No, follow the label: once a week

questions.stem: After a facial, which home-care advice is correct for a client in the Jamaican sun?
options: Use a sunscreen every day, even when it is cloudy
Use a sunscreen only on days she goes to the beach
Skip sunscreen because dark skin cannot be damaged
Use a body oil on the face instead of a sunscreen

questions.stem: Which is an honest way to describe a moisturiser?
options: It will cure your eczema in one week
It removes all wrinkles for good
It helps dry skin feel soft and smooth
It works for every person, guaranteed

questions.stem: Why must a therapist never claim that a beauty product treats a medical condition?
options: It is untrue and can stop the client getting proper medical care
It makes the product seem cheaper than the ones in the pharmacy
It takes too long to explain at the front desk to a busy client
It means the salon must give the client the product for free

questions.stem: A client asks about a skin problem you know nothing about. What is the best reply?
options: Guess a product so you do not look unsure
Say you do not know and suggest a doctor
Tell her that every cream will clear it up
Change the subject and talk about the price

questions.stem: Which document should a client get each time she buys a product?
options: A copy of the stock list
A client record card
A product price list
A receipt

questions.stem: Why should the salon's returns or exchange policy be explained or displayed?
options: So staff can refuse every return without a reason
So clients cannot complain to anyone about a product
So the salon does not have to give out receipts
So clients know their rights before they buy

questions.stem: A client says: 'That shampoo is too expensive.' What is a good reply?
options: Then you should go and buy a cheap one at the shop
You cannot have healthy hair without spending more
I understand. There is a smaller size that may suit
Everybody else buys it, so you should buy it too

questions.stem: A client says she does not want to buy anything today. What should you do?
options: Respect her choice and offer to note the product on her card
Keep telling her about the product over and over until she buys
Tell the next stylist to try to sell it to her at the desk
Refuse to book her next appointment until she buys one

questions.stem: A client returns a cream that made her skin itch. What should you do first?
options: Tell her it cannot be the cream and refuse to listen
Listen, ask her to stop using it, and tell the manager
Give her a stronger cream to stop the itching right away
Sell the same cream to her again in a bigger size

questions.stem: Why is a calm, polite manner important when a client complains?
options: It makes the client forget all about her problem
It means the salon never has to give a refund
It helps keep the client's trust and the salon's name
It lets the staff member end the talk much more quickly

questions.stem: What does FIFO mean for retail stock?
options: Fill in, fill out: refill the old bottles
First in, first out: sell older stock first
Fast items first out: sell the newest first
First in, final order: reorder when empty

questions.stem: A jar has a symbol of an open pot with '12M' on it. What does this mean?
options: The jar holds 12 millilitres of product
The product is only for clients over 12 years old
The jar must be stored for 12 months first
Use the product within 12 months of opening

questions.stem: What should be done with a product that is past its expiry date?
options: Take it off the shelf and follow the salon's procedure
Sell it at half price without telling the client why
Put it at the back of the shelf, behind the newer stock
Mix it with new stock of the same product

questions.stem: Where should retail products be stored?
options: In a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight
In the front window where the sun shines all day
On the floor of the stock room near the drain
Next to the dryer hood so they stay warm

questions.stem: How should aerosol cans such as hairspray be stored?
options: Next to the hot tools so they are easy to reach
In direct sun on the window display shelf
On top of the water heater in the back room
Away from heat and flames, as the label says

questions.stem: Which makes a good retail display?
options: Dusty shelves with products in no order
Open testers with no lids, left in the sun
Clean shelves, clear prices and tidy rows
Damaged boxes at the front to sell first

questions.stem: Why should every product on the shelf have a clear price label?
options: So staff can change the price for each client
So clients can see the cost and choose freely
So the product looks more costly than it is
So the supplier knows how much stock is left

questions.stem: Why does the salon count its retail stock regularly?
options: To give staff a reason to take a long break
To decide which clients may buy products
To know what is selling and when to reorder
To find which products have the nicest smell

questions.stem: A salon is registered for GCT. How should GCT be handled on a retail sale?
options: Add it only if the client asks for a receipt
Leave it off for regular clients as a favour
Add it at a rate the stylist chooses each day
Charge it at the current rate as required

questions.stem: A friend of a client asks what products the client bought. What should you do?
options: Show the friend the client's whole record card
Politely say you cannot share client details
Tell the friend, as long as she buys too
Post the list in the salon group chat

questions.stem: A client gets a cream in her eye while trying it. What is the right first aid?
options: Rinse the eye with plenty of clean, cool water
Rub the eye firmly with a tissue to get it all out
Put more cream around the eye to soothe it
Cover the eye and tell her to go back to work

questions.stem: A bottle of oil breaks on the salon floor. What should be done first?
options: Leave it for the cleaner who comes at night
Cover it with a towel and carry on selling
Warn people, then clean it up and dry the floor
Mop it into the drain with plenty of hot water

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: What do the letters SPF stand for on a sunscreen?
Name the skin type that is oily on the forehead, nose and chin (the T-zone) but normal or dry on the cheeks.
Which organ of the body, the largest one, do skin-care products look after?
What is the name for the company that makes a product and writes its instructions?
What is the word for a reason a client gives for not buying, such as the price?
Name the sheet a supplier gives that explains a product's hazards, safe storage and first aid.
What is the word for offering a client a bigger size or a better version of the product she asked for?
What is the word for removing dead skin cells from the skin's surface, for example with a scrub?
What word on a label means a product is made so that it is unlikely to block the pores?
A shampoo bottle says 250 ml. What unit does 'ml' stand for?
Name the Jamaican government body that helps consumers with their rights and complaints.
What is the name for a small free amount of product a client may take home to try?
What is the name for the date after which a product should not be sold or used?
What do the letters GCT stand for?
What is the word for the advice a client is given on caring for her hair or skin at home after a salon service?

essays.stem: Describe how you would find out a new client's needs before recommending a skin-care product to her.
essays.modelAnswer: I would greet the client, take her to a quiet area and explain that I will ask a few questions so that I can suggest the right product. I would use open questions, such as 'How does your skin feel by the end of the day?' and 'What products do you use now?' I would listen without interrupting and look at her skin in good light to see if it is dry, oily, combination or sensitive. I would ask about allergies, skin conditions, medicines and any reactions she has had before, and check her record card. If I see broken, infected or very irritated skin, I would not sell a product for it and would suggest she see a doctor. Then I would sum up what she told me to check that I understood, and only then recommend one or two products that match her needs and budget. I would write the advice and any purchase on her record card.
markingPoints: Explains the purpose and uses open questions, listening without interrupting
Looks at the skin to identify the skin type
Asks about allergies, conditions, medicines and past reactions; checks the record card
Does not sell for broken or infected skin and refers to a doctor
Sums up the needs before recommending, and records the advice and purchase

essays.stem: Choose one retail hair or skin product. Describe how you would present it to a client, using its features, its benefits, how to use it and its price.
essays.modelAnswer: I would choose a moisturising leave-in conditioner for a client with dry, relaxed hair. First I link it to what she told me: her hair feels dry and breaks when she combs it. I give the features: it contains shea butter and coconut oil and comes in a 250 ml bottle. Then I turn each feature into a benefit for her: the oils help her hair feel softer, so it is easier to comb and is less likely to break. I show her how to use it: a small amount, about the size of a coin, worked through damp hair from the middle to the ends, used as the label says. I put a little on the back of her hand with a clean spatula so she can feel the texture. I tell her the price clearly, including GCT at the current rate if the salon is registered, and mention any smaller size. Then I ask if she has any questions and let her decide without pressure.
markingPoints: Links the product to the needs found in consultation
Gives at least one feature and turns it into a benefit for the client
Explains how much to use and how, following the label
Demonstrates hygienically (clean spatula, back of hand)
States the price clearly and lets the client decide without pressure

essays.stem: Explain why you must ask about allergies and skin conditions before recommending a product, and what you should do if a client has a reaction to something she bought.
essays.modelAnswer: Some ingredients, such as nut oils, fragrance, dyes or preservatives, can cause allergies. A product can also make a skin condition such as eczema, an infection or broken skin worse. If I ask first and read the ingredient list, I can avoid selling something that may harm the client. If she has a condition I am not trained to deal with, I should not recommend a product for it but suggest she see a doctor. If a client comes back with a reaction, such as redness, itching, swelling or a rash, I listen calmly and do not argue. I tell her to stop using the product at once and to rinse the area with cool water. If the reaction is bad, spreading or near the eyes, she should get medical help. I tell the manager, write the reaction and the product's name and batch on her record card, and follow the salon's policy on returns and reporting.
markingPoints: Explains that ingredients can cause allergies or make conditions worse
Asks first and checks the ingredient list before recommending
Refers conditions it cannot treat to a doctor
For a reaction: stop use, rinse, medical help if severe
Tells the manager, records the reaction and product, and follows the salon's policy

essays.stem: A client is buying a permanent hair colour to use at home. Describe the safety advice you would give her.
essays.modelAnswer: I would tell her to read the maker's instructions fully before she starts and to follow them exactly. She must do a skin test as the maker says, often 48 hours before colouring, even if she has used the product before, and not colour if there is any redness, itching or swelling. A strand test, if the maker asks for one, shows how the colour will look. She should check her scalp first and not colour if it has cuts, sores or irritation. She must wear the gloves in the pack, work in a room with fresh air, and keep the colour away from her eyes. If it gets in her eyes, she should rinse them at once with plenty of clean water and get medical help. She must time the colour as the instructions say, never mix it with another brand, and throw away any mixed colour that is left. Products should be stored out of reach of children.
markingPoints: Read and follow the maker's instructions
Skin test as the maker says (often 48 hours) and strand test if required
Check the scalp for cuts or irritation and do not colour if present
Gloves, ventilation, keep away from eyes; rinse eyes and get help if needed
Time correctly, never mix brands, discard leftovers, store safely away from children

essays.stem: Explain why retail advice must always be honest, and give examples of claims a therapist should never make.
essays.modelAnswer: Honest advice builds trust. A client who gets a product that really suits her will come back and tell her friends, but one who feels tricked will not return and may complain. It is also unfair and can break consumer law to give false information about a product. A therapist should only say what the product can really do, as the maker's information shows. She should never say a cream will cure eczema, acne or any medical problem, or that it will remove all wrinkles for ever. She should not promise that a product works for every person, or say that a cheap product is dangerous just to sell a costly one. She should not hide the price or the GCT, or push a client to buy something she does not need. If she does not know the answer to a question, she should say so and find out, or suggest that the client see a doctor or pharmacist.
markingPoints: Honest advice builds trust and repeat business
False claims are unfair and can break consumer law
Never claims to cure a medical condition or give permanent results
No false guarantees, hidden prices or pressure selling
Says when she does not know, finds out or refers to a doctor or pharmacist

essays.stem: A client likes a serum but says it costs too much. Describe how you would handle this without putting pressure on her.
essays.modelAnswer: I would stay calm and friendly and show that I understand, for example by saying, 'I understand, it is a lot to spend.' I would not argue or make her feel bad. I would remind her of the benefit she wanted, such as more even skin tone, and explain how long the bottle lasts if she uses it as the label says, so she can see the cost per week. I could offer a smaller size, a lower-priced product that does a similar job, or a sample if the salon has one. I could also offer to write the product on her record card so she can buy it on her next visit. In the end, the choice is hers. If she still says no, I thank her and keep giving her the same good service, so she feels respected and is happy to come back.
markingPoints: Stays calm, shows understanding and does not argue
Restates the benefit the client wanted
Explains value, such as how long the product lasts
Offers options: smaller size, lower-priced product or sample, or a note on her card
Accepts her decision politely and keeps good service

essays.stem: A client returns a shampoo, saying it did not work for her. Describe the steps you would follow to deal with her complaint.
essays.modelAnswer: I would greet her politely, take her to a quiet spot and listen to the whole complaint without interrupting. I would thank her for telling us and say I am sorry the product did not meet her needs. Then I would ask questions to understand the problem: how she used it, how much and how often, and what result she expected. If she had a skin or scalp reaction, I would tell her to stop using it and see a doctor if needed. I would check the receipt and the salon's returns policy, and if I cannot decide, I would call the manager. Possible solutions are an exchange for a more suitable product, a refund, or advice on using it the right way, as the policy allows. I would record the complaint and the outcome on her record card and in the complaints book, and tell the manager so the team can learn from it.
markingPoints: Listens fully and politely, in private, and apologises
Asks questions to find the cause, including how it was used
Checks for a reaction and advises stopping use or seeing a doctor if needed
Checks the receipt and returns policy; involves the manager where needed
Offers a fair solution and records the complaint and outcome

essays.stem: Describe how to set up and look after a retail display in a salon.
essays.modelAnswer: First I clear the shelves and clean them with a suitable cleaner, wearing gloves and following the maker's instructions. I check every product for its expiry date, the open-jar symbol, damage and broken seals, and I take out anything out of date or damaged and deal with it as the salon's procedure says. I group products by type, such as hair, skin, nails and sun care, with the labels facing out. I put older stock at the front so it sells first (first in, first out) and new stock behind. Every product has a clear price label. Testers are kept clean, with lids on, and clients are offered a clean spatula. The display is out of direct sunlight and away from heat, and aerosols are kept away from hot tools. I dust and tidy the display every day, refill it from the stock room, and record what is sold so the manager knows when to reorder.
markingPoints: Cleans the shelves safely before setting up
Checks expiry dates, open-jar symbols and damage; removes unsuitable stock
Groups products neatly with clear price labels
Rotates stock first in, first out
Stores out of sun and heat, keeps testers hygienic, tidies and records sales daily

essays.stem: Compare the home-care products you would suggest for a client with dry, relaxed hair and for a client with an oily scalp.
essays.modelAnswer: Relaxed hair has been chemically treated, so it is often dry and easy to break. For this client I would suggest a gentle moisturising shampoo, a rich conditioner, a weekly deep conditioning treatment as the label says, and a light leave-in or oil for the ends. If she uses a flat iron or blow-dryer, she needs a heat protection product. A satin scarf or bonnet at night helps stop breakage. For a client with an oily scalp, I would suggest a balancing or clarifying shampoo, used as often as the label says. She should put conditioner on the lengths and ends only, not on the scalp, and avoid heavy oils and greases on the roots. The main difference is that dry, relaxed hair needs more moisture and protection, while an oily scalp needs gentle cleansing and lighter products. For both clients I would check for allergies and explain how much to use.
markingPoints: Dry relaxed hair: moisturising shampoo, rich conditioner, deep treatment
Dry relaxed hair: heat protection and night protection such as a satin scarf
Oily scalp: balancing or clarifying shampoo used as the label says
Oily scalp: conditioner on lengths only, avoid heavy oils on the roots
States the main difference and checks allergies and use for both

essays.stem: Describe how you would complete a retail sale once a client has decided to buy a product.
essays.modelAnswer: First I check that I have the right product and size, and that the seal is not broken and it is in date. I tell the client the total price clearly. If the salon is registered for GCT, the price includes GCT charged at the current rate. I take payment the way the salon allows, such as cash or card, count any change back to her, and give her a receipt. I remind her briefly how to use the product, how much to use and what to do if she has a reaction. I tell her the salon's returns or exchange policy. I bag the product neatly and thank her for her purchase. Afterwards I record the product on her record card, so the next stylist knows what she uses, and update the stock sheet. I keep her details private and never share them with anyone who does not need them.
markingPoints: Checks the product, size, seal and date
States the total price clearly, with GCT at the current rate if registered
Takes payment correctly and gives a receipt
Repeats how to use the product and explains the returns policy
Records the sale on the record card and stock sheet, keeping details private

practical1.title: Role play: consultation and retail product advice
practical1.brief: As a group, set up a retail advice area in the Centre's salon and role-play product consultations. The assessor gives each member a client card (for example: dry relaxed hair and a flat iron used daily; oily skin that shines by midday; dry cuticles after a manicure; sun care for a beach wedding in Negril; a client who says the price is too high). Take turns so that every member plays the therapist once, the client once and the observer once. As the therapist: greet the client, ask open questions, check for allergies and skin or scalp conditions, fill in a consultation and record card, recommend one or two suitable products with a feature and a benefit for each, demonstrate one product on the back of the hand with a clean spatula, give instructions and aftercare advice, handle one objection politely, and complete a practice sale with a written receipt. The observer fills in an observation sheet. Use made-up names on all forms. Photos show only hands, products and forms, never faces, unless the person agrees and the Centre allows it. Photograph each stage and add the photos to the group's practical.
materials: Client cards from the assessor (one per member)
Blank consultation and record cards, and an observation sheet for each round
Retail products or empty packaging with labels from the Centre's stock
Disposable spatulas, tissues and a lined bin
A practice receipt book, a calculator and pens
Hand sanitiser and a phone or camera for photos
photos: The retail advice area set up, with products grouped and priced
A completed consultation and record card for each member (made-up names)
A product being shown on the back of a hand with a clean spatula (hands only)
The products chosen for each client card, with labels facing out
A completed practice receipt for each member
The area cleaned and the products put back
checklist: Greeted the client politely and explained the purpose of the questions
Used open questions and listened without interrupting
Checked for allergies and skin or scalp conditions, and referred to a doctor where needed
Recommended suitable products and gave at least one feature and one benefit for each
Demonstrated hygienically, with a clean spatula used once and on the back of the hand
Gave clear instructions for use and correct aftercare advice
Handled the objection calmly and without pressure
Completed the record card and practice receipt accurately
Made no medical claims or false promises about any product
Took a full part as therapist, client and observer
safety: Never put a product on broken, sore or irritated skin; check the client card for allergies before any demonstration
Use each spatula once only and keep tester lids on; wash or sanitise hands before and after each demonstration
If product gets in an eye, rinse at once with plenty of clean water and tell the assessor
Follow the maker's instructions and the Centre's rules for every product
Keep the floor clear and wipe up any spill at once

practical2.title: Set up a retail display with product information cards
practical2.brief: As a group, set up and stock a retail display in the Centre's salon, then make product information cards and an aftercare leaflet for clients. Give each member one product group to lead (for example hair care, skin care, nail care, sun care and men's grooming), and work together on the whole display. In stages: (1) take everything off the shelves, then clean them safely; (2) check every product for its expiry date, open-jar symbol, broken seals and damage, list any problem items on a stock sheet and set them aside in a labelled box for the assessor; (3) arrange the products by group, older stock at the front (first in, first out), labels facing out, with a clear price label on each and a note that prices include GCT at the current rate where it applies; (4) each member writes one product information card for a product in their group, giving what it is, one feature, one benefit, how to use it and any warnings; (5) together, make a one-page aftercare leaflet or poster for one service, such as a relaxer or a manicure; (6) count the stock and fill in the stock sheet. Photograph each stage and add the photos to the group's practical.
materials: The Centre's retail stock or labelled practice packaging, with some out-of-date or damaged items placed by the assessor
Shelf cleaner, cloths and disposable gloves
Price labels, card for product information cards, markers and a ruler
Chart paper or A4 paper for the aftercare leaflet or poster
A blank stock sheet and a labelled box for problem items
A phone or camera for photos
photos: The problem items set aside in the labelled box, with the stock sheet beside them
The finished display, grouped and priced, from the front
Each member's product information card, close up
The finished aftercare leaflet or poster
checklist: Cleaned the shelves safely, wearing gloves and following the cleaner's instructions
Checked expiry dates, open-jar symbols, seals and damage, and found the problem items
Placed older stock in front of newer stock (first in, first out)
Arranged their product group neatly, labels out, with a clear price on each
Kept aerosols and heat-sensitive products out of sun and away from heat
Wrote an accurate, honest product card with a feature, a benefit, how to use it and warnings
Helped write correct aftercare advice with no medical claims
Counted stock accurately and filled in the stock sheet
Worked well with the group and left the area tidy
safety: Use the shelf cleaner as the maker's instructions say, with gloves and fresh air; never mix cleaning products
Use a proper step stool for high shelves; never climb on chairs or trolleys
Lift heavy boxes with bent knees and a straight back, or ask for help
If glass breaks, do not pick it up with bare hands; sweep it up and wrap it before putting it in the bin
Keep aerosols away from heat, flames and direct sunlight
